description: Golden Set v1, frozen on 2026-10-14. 36 cases agreed by Gonçalo Augusto (reviewer 1, every case) with a second, non-blind review by Rodrigo (comments that changed GS-01, GS-08 and GS-15). Built from golden_set_candidates.json (candidates drafted by the coding assistant), reviewed and edited by the group; decisions, dates and reasons per case are in golden_set_review.md. Never edit this file: a correction is a new version (golden_set_v2.json) with an entry in ITERATION_LOG.md.

cases.question: What is Searle's Chinese Room thought experiment meant to show?
key_facts: Manipulating symbols by rules (syntax) is not the same as understanding meaning (semantics).
It is an argument against strong AI: behaving intelligently does not give a program a mind.

cases.question: When a model is trained with gradient descent, what happens if the learning rate is too large or too small?
key_facts: If the learning rate is too large, the weight corrections grow without limit.
If the learning rate is too small, convergence is very slow.
A constant learning rate can leave the weights oscillating around the best solution; one that decreases over time makes them converge.

cases.question: How does Nick Bostrom define superintelligence, and what pathways to it are discussed?
key_facts: Superintelligence is any intellect that greatly exceeds human cognitive performance in virtually all domains of interest.
Pathways: biological cognition, whole brain emulation and artificial intelligence.
When or whether it is possible is an open question.

cases.question: What is the vanishing gradient problem, and why does ReLU help with it?
key_facts: The sigmoid saturates for large inputs, so its derivative approaches 0.
In backpropagation gradients are multiplied layer by layer, so many small gradients shrink towards zero.
ReLU does not saturate for positive inputs and is computationally cheap.

cases.question: What did the Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study of knowledge workers suggest about using AI?
key_facts: The study surveyed 319 knowledge workers about how they used AI.
The press reported it as Microsoft admitting AI is making us dumb.
Making life easier with AI has a price.

cases.question: How does prompt caching lower cost, and why can a timestamp at the top of a system prompt stop it from working?
key_facts: A later call that starts with a byte-identical prefix is billed at a fraction of the input price and answers faster.
The match is an exact prefix, so one changed character invalidates everything after it.
Order the context stable first and volatile last; a timestamp at the top silently disables caching.

cases.question: What is the difference between precision and recall, and why can accuracy be misleading?
key_facts: Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of the ones flagged, how many were right.
Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of the ones that mattered, how many were caught.
Accuracy lies on imbalanced data because the large true-negative box does the work.

cases.question: What is the difference between an LLM workflow and an LLM agent?
key_facts: A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths written by a developer.
An agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool use at runtime.
The difference is not intelligence but who decides the next step.

cases.question: What does Cohen's kappa measure, and why is raw agreement between annotators not enough?
key_facts: Raw agreement flatters: annotators can agree often just by chance on an imbalanced set.
Kappa subtracts the agreement expected by chance: (po - pe)/(1 - pe).
Below 0.4 the labels are not usable; the fix is to rewrite the label definitions.

cases.question: In a transformer, how does attention decide which earlier words matter for the next token?
key_facts: For every token it produces, the model re-weights all the tokens it has already seen.
Attention is learned, not programmed, and its cost grows with the square of the context length.
A transformer is a stack of layers, each doing attention and a feed-forward step.

cases.question: According to Kotter and Schlesinger, why do people resist organisational change?
key_facts: Parochial self-interest.
Misunderstanding and lack of trust.
Different assessments of costs and benefits.
Low tolerance for change.

cases.question: What is the cost per verified outcome, and which costs go into it?
key_facts: Cost per verified outcome = (model + retrieval + verification + escalation + rework + governance cost) divided by outcomes accepted by a human or a defined automatic test.
In the worked customer-service example, model inference is only about 1.5% of the cost; escalation and rework dominate.
It is tracked with volume, containment, verification rate and defect escape rate.

cases.question: What happened with Klarna's AI customer service assistant after its launch?
key_facts: In February 2024 the assistant handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month, equated to about 700 full-time agents (company-reported).
In May 2025 the CEO said the focus on cost had lowered quality, and humans were reintroduced for disputes, fraud and hardship.
AI handles the simple tier while human service becomes a premium tier.

cases.question: What do the letters in Prosci's ADKAR model stand for?
key_facts: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement.
ADKAR describes the phases individuals go through in a change.

cases.question: For a company, how do retrieval and fine-tuning compare in cost, time to value and risk, and when does each one fit?
key_facts: Retrieval has medium cost and high control, takes 1–3 months, and fits when answers must be traceable to the company's own sources; retrieval quality becomes the ceiling.
Fine-tuning or adapters have a medium-high recurring cost, risk deprecation when the base model moves, take 2–4 months, and fit when format and behaviour matter more than knowledge.

cases.question: What are the five checks for judging the quality of a source?
key_facts: Authority, relevance, timeliness, independence and traceability.
Weak sources can still be leads but should not become evidence.

cases.question: What is the tool-first trap when choosing an AI tool, and what should come first instead?
key_facts: Tool-first thinking names a tool before the task, data, risk, output and success criteria are clear.
State the work first, then choose the category and the tool.
Tool selection starts with a bounded task, narrow enough to test, review and improve.

cases.question: In which situations should a business professional not use an AI tool at all?
key_facts: When the data is restricted without approval.
When the decision is high-stakes without qualified review.
When there is no verification path, a false-authority risk, or unclear ownership.

cases.question: What should an evidence table record for each important claim in AI-assisted research?
key_facts: The claim, source, date, exact evidence, whether it was verified, and notes.
Each claim follows the chain claim, source, evidence, check, limit.
Build the table before writing the brief.

cases.question: When should I write a message myself rather than have an AI draft it?
key_facts: Condolences or bad news, disciplinary or performance letters, personal apologies, resignations or thanks, and anything read as personal.
Authorship is the message and discovery damages trust.
If the reader would feel worse on learning it was generated, generate nothing.

cases.question: A document I give an AI assistant could contain hidden instructions. What is this risk called and how can I reduce it?
key_facts: It is (indirect) prompt injection: instructions inside source text the model reads.
Separate instructions from source material and treat source text as data, not instructions.
Wording alone is not enough: limit permissions and require approval for consequential actions.

cases.question: Does telling an AI to act as an expert make its answers more accurate?
key_facts: A role changes vocabulary, register, level of detail and format.
A role does not grant expertise or factual accuracy the model does not have.
Say what you want done; keep accountability with an authorised person.

cases.question: How do I compare two versions of a prompt fairly?
key_facts: Change one thing at a time.
Re-run the same inputs with the same settings and keep the conditions fixed.
One run or one better answer is not enough evidence.

cases.question: Why ask an AI for a table or a fixed schema instead of free text, and what can structure not guarantee?
key_facts: A fixed structure makes output easier to check, compare and process, and exposes missing information.
A schema or table constrains the shape, never the truth: it can still contain errors.
Compare every field with the source.

cases.question: How can I stop an AI from inventing facts that are not in the material I gave it?
key_facts: Supply the source and tell the tool to use only the supplied material.
Allow an escape hatch or abstention such as 'not stated' or 'cannot tell from these documents'.
Require a quote or source location for each claim, and check it yourself.

cases.question: Can I rely on an AI to review and correct its own answer?
key_facts: Self-correction without an outside signal often does not help: a model that got an answer wrong usually cannot tell.
It works when there is a reliable external check such as tests or a retrieved fact.
AI self-critique can suggest fixes, but the revised answer must still be verified against evidence.

cases.question: What is shadow AI, and why should a company worry about it?
key_facts: Shadow AI is staff using AI tools the organisation does not know about.
It is a risk of off-the-shelf tools, together with data leakage and privacy risk.

cases.question: What can go wrong when a company lets an AI answer its customers?
key_facts: It can overpromise, invent policy or admit liability; uncertain cases must be escalated.
The company stays liable for what its chatbot says (Moffatt v. Air Canada).
Quality and satisfaction can fall on complex or emotional cases (Klarna).
